claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of a stable passivating surface oxide layer.
The passivating oxide layer acts as a barrier to corrosion.
The passivating oxide layer acts as a barrier to mechanical wear.
Alloy composition influences the stability of the passivating oxide layer.
Environmental conditions influence the stability of the passivating oxide layer.
High temperatures, corrosive media, and mechanical stress constitute the harsh corrosive mechanical conditions considered by the hypothesis.
High-entropy alloys with optimized compositions will have lower combined wear-corrosion degradation than a matched baseline.
High-entropy alloys with optimized compositions will have a lower wear component of degradation than a matched baseline.
High-entropy alloys with optimized compositions will have a lower corrosion component of degradation than a matched baseline.
The prediction should hold for high-entropy alloys under harsh corrosive mechanical conditions.
The prediction may fail in less severe environments.
The prediction may fail outside the relevant alloy-composition ranges.
A controlled comparison of alloys with varying compositions can test the relationship between passive-layer stability and wear-corrosion resistance.
A lack of significant correlation between passive-layer formation or stability and simultaneous wear-corrosion resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of optimized compositions to improve resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
